candidates.name: opponent_forcing_moves
candidates.idea: The opponent has many forcing moves available next turn, especially checks and profitable captures, so the side to move is under pressure to react and may lose material or the initiative even when a calm static eval looks acceptable.

candidates.name: king_escape_squares
candidates.idea: A king with few safe adjacent flight squares is vulnerable to checks, back-rank mates, and mating nets; the network penalizes low king mobility even when no immediate mate is in the classical features.

candidates.name: attacked_knight_tempo
candidates.idea: A knight under attack, especially by a pawn or king, often has to retreat and cedes the initiative; the network values how many safe retreat squares the knight has and penalizes a kicked knight with few good squares.

candidates.name: enemy_king_stuck_in_center
candidates.idea: With queens on the board, a king stuck on the central e/d-file and still holding castling rights is a lasting tactical liability; the side to move is more optimistic when its own king is safer and the enemy king has not escaped.

candidates.name: pawn_tempo_on_high_piece
candidates.idea: A pawn break that attacks a queen, rook, or minor piece gains time and can be stronger than static evaluation suggests, especially in open early-middlegame positions.

candidates.name: forcing_initiative
candidates.idea: The side to move has a forcing resource: a capture, check, or one-move attack on a loose high-value piece. This initiative is worth more than the static classical estimate, because it forces the opponent to react.

candidates.name: opponent_pawn_on_seventh
candidates.idea: An enemy pawn one square from promotion is a decisive threat that raw material counts miss. Even if the side to move has checking resources, the opponent's queening pawn means the position is much worse than classical evaluation suggests.

candidates.name: opponent_checks_available
candidates.idea: The number of legal checking moves the opponent has. A high count means our king is dangerously exposed and the opponent can force the play, which explains why the network is more pessimistic than a static evaluation that only counts attacks on the king zone.

candidates.name: opponent_pieces_in_our_half
candidates.idea: The number of non-pawn, non-king opponent pieces that have penetrated into our half of the board. Enemy rooks, bishops, knights, and queens deep in our territory create threats and restrictions that a pure material or space count underestimates.

candidates.name: king_trap_check_pressure
candidates.idea: A cramped enemy king turns ordinary checks into mating threats. The network rewards checks that hit a king with few safe flight squares, an interaction that raw check counts and king-zone attack counts miss.

candidates.name: forcing_double_threat
candidates.idea: One forcing move can create two problems: check or capture plus an attack on another valuable piece. The network values this tactical overlap more than static material and separate check/capture counts.

candidates.name: back_rank_heavy_pressure
candidates.idea: Rooks and queens penetrating to the opponent's first two ranks, especially against a king with blocked or covered flight squares, create back-rank mating-net pressure that ordinary material and open-file scores underrate.

candidates.name: protected_checking_sacrifice
candidates.idea: A check is much more dangerous when the checking piece is protected, because the king cannot simply capture it; queen and knight checks landing on defended squares often force a mating net or win material.

candidates.name: pin_to_king_capturable_by_low_value
candidates.idea: An enemy piece pinned to its king is a real tactical target when it is also attacked by our king or a pawn, because it cannot move and can be taken by a low-value piece.

candidates.name: knight_king_zone_pressure
candidates.idea: Knights aimed at the enemy king zone are a concrete attacking asset; a knight attacking squares next to the king or key weak squares often creates mating threats that static evaluation misses.

candidates.name: development_deficit
candidates.idea: The side to move has more pieces still on their starting squares than the opponent. In open positions with many pieces, this undeveloped state lets the opponent seize the initiative, so the network is more pessimistic than a classical count of material and mobility suggests.

candidates.name: early_queen_sortie_penalty
candidates.idea: Moving the queen out early while minor pieces remain undeveloped is a classic opening mistake. The opponent can gain tempos by attacking the queen, leaving the side to move behind in development. The network penalizes this lost time more heavily than classical concepts.

candidates.name: tactical_pressure_against_us
candidates.idea: The opponent's pieces are actively attacking your pieces, forcing you to react and make defensive or retreating moves. This constant tactical pressure is a form of initiative that the network values more negatively than a classical evaluation, even when no piece is immediately hanging.

candidates.name: multi_target_forcing_pressure
candidates.idea: The network rewards a position when the side to move has a legal move that creates several immediate targets at once: checking, capturing, or attacking multiple enemy pieces with the moving piece. A quiet-looking move that points at two or more enemy units is treated as real pressure, not just mobility.

candidates.name: capture_fork_material
candidates.idea: The network values a capture that does more than win the captured piece: the capturing piece stays on a square where it forks or attacks several other valuable enemy units. This is the extra material the opponent cannot save after the capture, which static material and ordinary mobility miss.

candidates.name: latent_castling_resource
candidates.idea: The network treats an unused, legal castling option as a latent king-safety and rook-activation asset, especially when the king is still in the centre and the opponent no longer has the same resource. The side that can still castle later has a free tempo in reserve, even if the best move right now is not castling.

candidates.name: connected_advanced_pawn_mass
candidates.idea: In endgames, two adjacent advanced pawns create breakthrough and queening chances that are greater than the sum of two loose pawns; the network values the pawn phalanx itself, not just formally passed pawns.

candidates.name: king_escort_of_passed_pawn
candidates.idea: A passed pawn is much more dangerous when its own king is close enough to protect it and shepherd it toward promotion, especially if the enemy king is far from the pawn's path.

candidates.name: rook_cutoff_of_advanced_passer
candidates.idea: An active rook can be worth much more than its material when it cuts the enemy king off from an advanced passed pawn, either by controlling an intervening file or by controlling the queening rank.

candidates.name: development_lag
candidates.idea: Pieces still sitting on their starting squares represent lost tempo and a passive army. In sharp middlegames the network downgrades the side whose minor pieces are undeveloped more than raw mobility captures, because those pieces take several moves to become useful.

candidates.name: bad_minor_placement
candidates.idea: A knight on the rim or a bishop that stares at its own pawns is nearly a piece down. The network trusts the side whose knights and bishops stand on purposeful (central, pawn-compatible) squares, an asymmetry that aggregate mobility averages away.

candidates.name: enemy_infiltration
candidates.idea: Enemy pieces that have crossed into your half (a rook on the second rank, a queen in your camp, an advanced attacker) cramp your play and generate threats, while your own pieces stay home. The network penalizes the side whose opponent has infiltrated territory that its own pieces have not contested.

candidates.name: wing_capture_material_gain
candidates.idea: A capture on a wing file that wins a pawn or piece is worth more than the static estimate suggests, because it can open lines and create a lasting material or space edge. The side to move is more optimistic when such a wing capture is available.

candidates.name: quiet_loose_target_overload
candidates.idea: A quiet move that attacks an undefended enemy piece or pawn, or simultaneously attacks a defender and the piece it defends, creates a concrete material threat. This is stronger than static evaluation because the opponent must spend time solving the overload.

candidates.name: pawn_move_opens_rook_file
candidates.idea: A pawn move or pawn capture can vacate a file and suddenly give a friendly rook a clear line to an enemy pawn or piece. This discovered rook pressure is easy to miss and often makes the side to move more optimistic than static features imply.

candidates.name: winning_capture_material
candidates.idea: The side to move can win real material with a capture even after the most obvious recapture. This net swing (captured value minus the value of a captured attacker when the target is defended) is what a static material count misses, distinguishing a sound win from a merely available capture.

candidates.name: overloaded_defenders
candidates.idea: An enemy piece that is attacked is not really safe if every defender of it is also busy defending another attacked target. Such 'overloaded' defenders cannot hold everything, so the side to move has a fork/deflection win that a plain hanging-piece count never sees because the target is nominally defended.

candidates.name: enemy_king_flight_coverage
candidates.idea: Count how many of the squares right next to the enemy king (excluding ones blocked by its own pieces) are controlled by the side to move. High coverage means the king has no safe flight squares, so ordinary forcing moves become mating threats; this is a finer flight-square measure than raw king-zone attack counts.

candidates.name: pawn_tempo_vulnerability
candidates.idea: Pieces that are on squares where an enemy pawn can attack them (now or after a one- or two-square pawn advance) are liabilities: they can be kicked, losing time and giving the opponent the initiative. The network penalizes this more than a static material count.

candidates.name: unsupported_pieces
candidates.idea: Non-pawn pieces that are not defended by any of your pawns are less stable and more vulnerable to being attacked, even if not currently en prise. The network values pawn support for pieces more highly than classical material and mobility terms.

candidates.name: queen_tempo_vulnerability
candidates.idea: An exposed queen is a major liability: if it can be attacked by an enemy pawn (now or after a pawn advance), it must retreat, losing time. Even without a pawn attack, an unsupported queen off its starting square is a target. The network penalizes this lost tempo heavily.

candidates.name: protected_double_attack
candidates.idea: A move by a knight, bishop, or queen is extra valuable when it lands on a defended square and hits at least two enemy units, or gives check while hitting another unit. The protection turns a temporary double attack into a real initiative asset, not just a one-move threat.

candidates.name: productive_check
candidates.idea: A check is worth more than a generic check when the checking piece also attacks a loose enemy unit or is safe from capture. The opponent must solve king safety and material at the same time, so such checks are a concrete tempo gain rather than just a check count.

candidates.name: enemy_king_escape_limited
candidates.idea: The network rewards positions where the opposing king has few safe adjacent squares after accounting for our attacks and its own blockers. This is a concrete king-trapping/mating-net signal, distinct from simply counting attacks on the king zone.

unit_rules.rule: opp_P and rel_rank <= 5.5 and not isolated_pawn
not pawn_att_them and own_Q and rel_rank
not safe_from_own_pawns and dist_own_king > 6.5 and piece_reach <= 4.5

rules.name: Quiet position → pawn lever
rules.detail: a pawn push that attacks an enemy pawn

rules.name: Enemy king still in the centre → pawn lever
rules.detail: strike at the pawns in front of an uncastled king

rules.name: Quiet position → pawn sacrifice
rules.detail: push a pawn where it can be taken for free

rules.name: Behind in material → offer a trade
rules.detail: all of the excess is in lost positions
